title: We See And Hear What We Expect
author: Antonius Veritas
summary: Writing as Antonius Veritas, the author argues that what we expect from people quietly shapes what we perceive in them, so a mistaken judgment can cost a relationship or lead us to trust someone who means us harm. He opens with Othello, whose certainty about Desdemona makes every innocent detail look like proof of betrayal, and generalizes that we can be so sure who people are that everything they do seems to prove us right. He recounts his own habit of reading competence as arrogance and kindness as manipulation in a relationship, and the self-questioning that exposed it. His practical Stoic method is to check the emotional state you are judging from, to ask what someone meant before acting on an assumption, and to weigh repeated behavior over single moments. He recommends leading with love and curiosity while keeping sensitive matters private, applying the same scrutiny to people we like, and letting time and ordinary commitments reveal character.
points: Expectation works as a filter: if you think someone is great everything confirms it, and if you think they are untrustworthy even innocent behavior reads as a breach.
Before trusting your read of someone, ask whether jealousy, low mood or preoccupation is coloring it, since a day spent expecting the worst changes the meaning you give their words.
Asking 'What did you mean by that?' gives a person the chance to explain before you act on an assumption, and may show how much you added yourself.
Lead with love and openness, but keep sensitive information private, make small commitments first, and watch how people behave under pressure.
Trust and verify applies equally to people you enjoy, and a postmortem after a failed relationship improves judgment without prejudging the next person.
quotes: That’s the danger we have to recognize in ourselves- we can be so certain about who people are that everything they do seems to prove us right.
You dismiss advice that would have saved you because you don’t like the person giving it.

It’s tough to make your case to someone who has already decided what kind of person you are. You can’t dig yourself out of that hole. But it’s worth considering how often we put others in that position.
Their answer may reveal something unpleasant. It may also divulge how much we added to a sentence we barely thought about.
The best approach I’ve found in fine-tuning my expectations of others is to lead with love- to want the best for others, see the good in them, and wear my heart on my sleeve.

If I keep excusing their behavior because I think they’re great, I’m still seeing what I expect and it might blind me to sinister parts of their character. Trust and verify applies to the people whose company we enjoy too.
Ordinary commitments already reveal a great deal: how someone handles disagreement, responds when you say no, admits a mistake, or behaves when keeping their word becomes inconvenient.
